deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is German prose notes on ancient history, a continuous narrative carried over from folio 184 and on to folio 186. It looks like lecture or study notes, probably not composed by Gauss himself. The topic is Macedon under Philip V and Perseus, and Rome's growing control of Greece. In order, the page says:

(1) In 201 BC Rome declared war on Philip V. The war lasted 3 years.
(2) In 198 T. Quinctius Flamininus was sent against Philip. He won more by policy than by arms.
(3) In 197 he defeated Philip at Cynoscephalae, and Philip had to accept terms:
- withdraw his garrisons from the Greek cities;
- surrender his whole fleet;
- disband his armies, keeping only '500' armed men;
- pay 1000 talents;
- send his younger son Demetrius to Rome as a hostage;
- make no war without Roman consent.
(4) Rome then tried to set rivals beside Philip among the Greeks. Greek freedom was solemnly proclaimed (the Isthmian proclamation of 196), yet Roman armies stayed for 3 years and the Romans stirred up the tyrant Nabis against the Achaeans.
(5) During Rome's war with Antiochus the Great, Greece was again a theatre of war. The war ended in Rome's favour in 190.
(6) Philip secretly re-armed. In 181 he had Demetrius executed, his elder son Perseus being the designated heir. Philip died of grief in 179.
(7) Greece fell ever deeper into dependence on Rome. The Achaeans were still the strongest Greek power, but Rome kept other Greek peoples hostile to them.
(8) Aratus had perished. His successor Philopoemen died in 183.
(9) Perseus reigned 179–168. At first he renewed the treaty of friendship with Rome; the sentence continues on the next page.

The numerical tables on the next page (logarithms, 648000/π, angles such as 168°18'33") are unrelated to this text. Nothing on this page needs restating in modern notation.
errors: Term 3: the ancient sources (Polybius 18.44, Livy 33.30) limit Philip's army to 5000 men, not 500. Either the writer slipped or the numeral is a misreading.
Term 2: Philip had to give up all his decked warships except five plus the royal flagship, not literally his 'whole fleet'.
Demetrius was executed in 180 BC (some sources say 181/180), so '181' is slightly early or approximate.
The formal Roman declaration of the Second Macedonian War is usually dated 200 BC, not 201. Embassies and preparations did start in 201.
The war with Antiochus ended at Magnesia (winter 190/189) and the Peace of Apamea (188). '190' is acceptable only as the date of the decisive battle.
Rome actually waged war on Nabis in 195. The claim that the Romans 'incited Nabis against the Achaeans' is a tendentious simplification (it refers to Nabis's later attacks around 192).
Aratus died in 213 BC. Philopoemen's death in 183 (or 182) is correct, but the note's implied chronology of direct succession is loose.

results.what: Historical narrative of the Second Macedonian War, the Peace of 196 BC, the war with Antiochus III, and the succession of Philip V by Perseus
results.usually_credited_to: Polybius, Livy; standard 18th–19th century textbook material

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical history notes, apparently student or lecture notes on ancient history, with nothing of mathematical or Gauss-specific significance.

checkable.asserts: The war began in 201 and Flamininus was sent 3 years later, in 198 (as stated).
Roman troops staying '3 years' after the settlement ends around 194 BC, consistent with Flamininus's evacuation of Greece in 194.

transcription_corrections: 'das 3 Jahr darnach' should probably read 'der 3 Jahr dauerte' (the war lasted 3 years), followed by '198 wurde ...'.
'Achaeern[?] an die Seite zu setzen' reads better as 'Rivalen an die Seite zu setzen' (the Romans sought to set rivals beside him among the Greeks).
'Griechenland war nie[?] immer mehr Abhängigkeit' should read 'Griechenland war in immer mehr Abhängigkeit von Rom gekommen'.
'Flamminius' is the writer's spelling of Flamininus. The praenomen and nomen are Titus Quinctius.
'+Aratus war+' is an interlinear insertion above the line, completing 'Aratus war umgekommen'.
'Die Römer suchten ihn jetzt' is probably 'ihm' (dative).
